docs.title: What this is
docs.text:
A global atmospheric model called CAMS publishes a PM2.5 forecast for every point on Earth, Patiala included. At the CPCB station in Model Town it is badly wrong, and wrong by a different amount in every season: it reads close to four times the observed value in the monsoon and a little over one times in November. On a 0.4 degree grid, roughly 45 km per cell, a single number covers Patiala and everything around it. What it cannot know is what this particular station reads.

Pawan learns that difference. It takes the CAMS forecast for tomorrow, along with forecast weather and upwind fire detections, and applies a correction fitted on this station's own history. The output is one number: tomorrow's daily mean PM2.5 at Model Town.

docs.title: What counts as working
docs.text:
Raw CAMS is not the bar to beat, because almost anything beats it. The honest bar is persistence: assuming tomorrow looks like the most recent reading the station has published. The CPCB feed runs behind, so that reading is a few days old when the forecast goes out, and Pawan is always measured against persistence given the same reading it had. The proposal set a 10% reduction in error against it outside the burning season and 20% during it.

Both are met, the second across the 2025 and 2026 burning seasons, and Results has the current figures, regenerated every morning. The textbook version of persistence, which uses yesterday's reading, still beats Pawan. Nobody has yesterday's reading at forecast time, so it marks the cost of the publication lag rather than a competitor, but it is reported rather than left out.

See Tomorrow's forecast for the live service, Results for the full evaluation, Method for how it is measured and Data for what is in the table. The prototype report covers all of it in one place.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt
python code/ingest/run_daily.py      # needs OPENAQ_KEY, FIRMS_MAP_KEY
python code/evaluate.py              # backtest, writes data/metrics.json
python code/predict.py               # tomorrow and the outlook
python code/lab.py                   # the model lab
python -m pytest code/tests/ -q

The forecast uses nothing outside the standard library. requirements.txt carries pytest and ruff and nothing else. That is deliberate: the daily job has to keep running unattended until the end of the semester, and the least it can do is not depend on something that might change underneath it. The model lab's benchmarks need scikit-learn (requirements-lab.txt), and run in a step of their own that cannot stop the daily commit.

The job runs every day through GitHub Actions and commits the result, so data/daily.csv is the real dataset and its history is the commit log.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The website is static on purpose. Nothing has to stay running for it to work, and a sleeping server cannot take it down. The API sits beside it for programs rather than people: it serves the same data files the site is built from, and does the one thing a static page cannot do for someone else, which is run the model on inputs they supply.

It is written with FastAPI, which builds the interactive documentation from the code's own types.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements-api.txt
python code/api.py

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs. Each endpoint can be tried from that page.

Every request reads the files in data/ fresh, so the answers move with the daily job without a restart. The API never writes anything.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method Path What it returns GET /forecast Tomorrow's forecast, its likely range and advice, and the two days after. If there is no forecast, the reason. GET /forecasts Every forecast on record with what was measured. Filters: start, end, scored, limit. GET /models The model lab's leaderboard, best backtest error first, with each model's live record. GET /health The newest station reading and how old it is, the last forecast and when it was issued, and whether the feed has gone stale. POST /whatif The shipped model's forecast for inputs you supply.

All figures are daily mean PM2.5 in µg/m³. Bands follow the CPCB National AQI breakpoints.

docs.title: What if
docs.text:
/whatif takes the same readings the daily forecast is built from:

{
  "cams": 65.2,
  "reading": 68.8,
  "temp": 19.58,
  "rh": 62.08,
  "wind_speed": 9.49,
  "wind_dir": 311.91,
  "fires": 123,
  "day": "2026-11-16"
}

These are 16 November's real inputs, and the answer is the forecast the daily job issued for that day, to the hundredth:

{
  "day": "2026-11-16",
  "pm25": 52.53,
  "band": "Satisfactory",
  "likely_range": [34.06, 91.24],
  "extrapolating": [],
  "model_reading_age": 2
}

Two kinds of input are treated differently.

  • Impossible inputs are refused with a 422: humidity above 100%, a negative fire count, a bearing outside 0 to 360.
  • Inputs outside what the model was fitted on are answered, but listed under extrapolating, with the lowest and highest value in the fitted rows. A linear model keeps going in a straight line long after the physics stops agreeing, so a number built on these deserves suspicion. Asked about 20,000 fires, ten times anything in the record, the model still says Moderate, and the answer says why not to trust it.

model_reading_age is the age of station reading the model was fitted for, counted from the day forecast. A reading of another age is weighed as if it were that one; see Method.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: Everything lives in one file, data/daily.csv, one row per calendar day in IST. It is committed to git, so its history is the commit log and any correction is visible as a diff. At this size that is worth more than a database.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text: Column Meaning date The day the row describes, IST. obs_pm25 Observed daily mean PM2.5 at Model Town, µg/m³. The target. obs_hours How many hourly readings that mean is built from. bootstrap.py did not record it; extend_history.py fills it in wherever the fetched reading matches the stored one. cams_pm25 CAMS global PM2.5 forecast for this day, daily mean, µg/m³. cams_issue_date The day that forecast was issued. Blank means backfilled. temp_mean Daily mean 2 m temperature, °C. rh_mean Daily mean relative humidity, %. wind_speed_mean Daily mean 10 m wind speed, km/h. wind_dir_mean Daily mean 10 m wind bearing, degrees. Vector mean, not arithmetic. fire_count VIIRS fire detections in the upwind box that day. ingested_at When the row was last written, IST.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Observations come from OpenAQ v3, location 5544, sensor 12235142. The station exposes a second PM2.5 sensor, 15243, which has not reported since October 2022 but still serves its old series on request. Both ids are pinned in config.py so nobody reverses the choice by accident. The v3 aggregate endpoints ignore parameters they do not recognise rather than rejecting them, so every window is filtered again client-side.

Forecast and weather come from Open-Meteo, cams_global domain for PM2.5. CAMS global publishes every 12 hours at three-hourly resolution; the hourly series is interpolated from that, and the daily mean is taken over the interpolated hours.

Fires come from NASA FIRMS, VIIRS products, over the box 73.8, 27.5, 77.7, 32.6 — Punjab and Haryana upwind of Patiala. The near-real-time products only keep a rolling window and answer with an empty CSV rather than an error outside it, so the ingest picks a product per date from the availability endpoint and records nothing when none of them reaches back far enough.

Only the count goes into the dataset. The positions of the last two days' fires are kept separately in data/fires.json, overwritten every morning, for the dashboard map. Each fire is cut down to latitude, longitude, fire radiative power and the VIIRS confidence flag.

docs.title: Two kinds of row, and why it matters
docs.text:
Rows arrive by two routes and they are not equivalent.

Live rows are written each morning by code/ingest/run_daily.py. They carry a cams_issue_date, which proves the forecast existed before the day it describes. These are the rows the final evaluation rests on.

Backfilled rows come from archives. The first 92 days were seeded by scripts/bootstrap.py, the history back to February 2025 was added by scripts/extend_history.py, and the meteorology and fire counts for all of them were filled in by scripts/backfill_history.py. They have no issue date, because the CAMS archive serves a series stitched from many model runs and does not say which run any given value came from. The lead time is therefore unknown and probably shorter than a real day-ahead forecast, which makes these rows mildly optimistic.

They are still used, because a year and a half of slightly optimistic history, including the whole 2025 burning season, beats a few weeks of perfect history and a model that has never seen an October.

The 92-day start was a mistake worth recording. bootstrap.py asked for past_days=92 on the belief that this was as far back as the CAMS archive went. It is only the ceiling on that one parameter: an explicit start_date reaches back to August 2022. The sensor has reported since February 2025, so the 2025 burning season was available from the first day of the project. What they are not allowed to do is quietly become the headline number. features.py marks each row with live, the test suite refuses any row whose issue date is not strictly before its target day, and the honest comparison is the live-only subset once enough of it exists.

scripts/backfill_history.py prints which archive answered, and that is recorded in the journal, because it changes how the meteorology should be read.

docs.title: Holes
docs.text:
Gaps are left as blank cells rather than interpolated. A missing day is information — usually the station was down — and filling it in with a plausible number would hide that from the model and from us. features.py drops any row without a complete feature vector and reports the per-column count, so a small training set can be traced to the column responsible instead of being blamed on the model.

The CPCB feed also runs late, by an amount that has moved over the semester: three days in August, batches every few days in early October, about one day since late October. The forecast does not assume a lag. It uses the freshest valid reading on file and a model fitted at that reading's age. See Method.

docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending: tomorrow becomes the target
    Pending --> Skipped: inputs missing, or no reading within 7 days
    Pending --> Issued: inputs complete

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text: Decision Instead of Why CSV committed to git A database One file of a few hundred rows; the commit log is a free audit trail of every change to the data Static site, separate optional API A web app with a server Nothing to keep alive; the dashboard cannot go down with a server Forecast path in the standard library scikit-learn throughout The daily job runs unattended for months; the less it depends on, the less can change underneath it Ridge regression in log space Trees or a neural network Beats them on about 500 days of data, in the lab's own comparison; its arithmetic can be shown exactly on the dashboard One model per reading age One model, whatever the reading's age A model fitted on two-day-old readings would weigh a five-day-old one wrongly Forecasts frozen when issued Recomputed as the model improves The track record is of what was actually claimed A written promotion rule Shipping whichever model scores best A model can win one exam by luck; the rule asks for several

docs.title: Testing

docs.title: The problem, precisely
docs.text:
On the morning of day D-1, produce the daily mean PM2.5 at Model Town for day D.

The word morning is doing real work there. It fixes what the model is allowed to know, and that turns out to be less than the proposal assumed.

docs.title: What is actually available at issue time
docs.text:
The daily job is scheduled for 08:00 IST. GitHub starts scheduled jobs late when it is busy, and in practice the run lands in the afternoon, so each forecast records the time it was actually issued. Four backup runs through the day (code/due.py) do the work again only if that run went out without a forecast, or if by evening it has not run at all. They never run ahead of it, so a backup that fires on time cannot forecast from a staler reading. Whenever the job runs, the CAMS and weather forecasts for tomorrow are already out. The station's own readings are a different matter.

The CPCB feed runs behind, and by how much has changed over the semester. On 17 August the newest published day was 14 August, three days behind. In early October readings arrived in batches every few days. Since late October each day has been published by the next afternoon.

For most of the project the lag was a fixed three days, measured in August. When the feed sped up, that rule kept throwing away readings the job already had. On 2 November the forecast for the 3rd was built from 30 October's 11.4 µg/m³ while 31 October (79) and 1 November (106) were already in daily.csv. On 30 October no forecast went out at all: the one day the rule allowed was thin, and the days behind it had never been published.

So the age of the reading is no longer assumed. It is counted from the target day, so a reading from D-2 is two days old. That is the youngest a day-ahead forecast can have, because the issue day is not over when the job runs. Each morning the job finds the freshest valid reading on file (features.freshest_age) and forecasts with a model fitted on readings of exactly that age (features.build(age=...)). A model fitted on two-day-old readings has learnt how much a two-day-old reading is worth, and it is never handed a five-day-old one. Past config.OBS_MAX_AGE, seven days, there is no forecast.

The headline backtest is run at config.OBS_REFERENCE_AGE, two days, which is what the feed delivers now. The model lab scores the other ages as well, so a slower feed shows up as a measured cost.

This matters more than it sounds, because it changes what "persistence" means.

docs.title: Persistence, twice
docs.text:
Persistence normally means tomorrow equals today. That is the number in the proposal: MAE 6.5 µg/m³ over 89 day-pairs. It is a fair textbook baseline and it is what the marks were promised against.

It is also not available to us. Predicting D from D-1 requires knowing D-1, and at issue time we do not. So the backtest reports both:

  • persistence — obs on D-1. The textbook bar, and the one the proposal targets. Uses information the model cannot have.
  • persistence_operational — the reading of the same age the model gets, two days old at the reference age. The same information set the model has.

The first is the honest target. The second is the honest comparison. Reporting only one of them would be a way of choosing the answer in advance, so both go in data/metrics.json.

Climatology and raw CAMS are carried alongside as sanity checks. Climatology is computed causally — the mean of everything observed strictly before the day in question, not the mean of the whole record, which would leak.

docs.title: Backtest
docs.text:
code/evaluate.py walks forward one day at a time. For each target day it fits on every usable row strictly before that day, predicts one value, and moves on. No shuffled split, because the rows are a time series and shuffling lets the model see its own future.

The ridge penalty alpha is chosen inside each fit, on the most recent fifth of that fit's training window. Choosing it once on the whole record would leak the test period into a hyperparameter — a small leak, but the kind that quietly inflates every number downstream.

The first MIN_TRAIN = 40 rows are used for fitting only, never scored. Below that the fit is noise.

Reported per run: MAE, RMSE, bias, correlation, and the rate at which the prediction lands in the correct CPCB National AQI band. The last one matters because a person reading a forecast wants to know whether tomorrow is Satisfactory or Poor, not whether the error was 7.2 or 7.4.

Scores are split into calm and burning seasons, since the targets differ and the two regimes barely resemble each other.

docs.title: Why ridge, and why by hand
docs.text:
The correction is linear in the features, with an L2 penalty, fitted through the normal equations and solved by Gaussian elimination. Roughly eighty lines in code/model.py.

scikit-learn would be two lines. It would also put numpy, scipy and a compiled BLAS in the path of a job that has to run unattended every morning until November. The model is small enough that writing it out keeps the whole pipeline standard-library only, and a fitted model is then just the numbers in data/model.json — reproducible without installing anything.

The features are few and mostly logged, so a linear model is not obviously the wrong shape. The model lab, below, now tests that directly: on this much data a random forest, gradient boosting and a small neural network all score worse than the ridge fit.

docs.title: The week 5 review
docs.text:
The first fitted model lost to textbook persistence by 22.6% and, worse, had started drifting downward while the station was climbing. Pulling it apart found five separate faults, and the current model is what came out of fixing them.

  • The meteorology was never switched on. The backfill had been run weeks earlier and the fit was still reading CAMS, lagged observations and a seasonal term. Wind and fire counts, the two things most likely to matter in October, had never been tested.
  • doy_sin and doy_cos were not measuring seasonality. With four months of data a day-of-year term cannot tell a season from a trend, and these had learnt "PM2.5 falls through the monsoon". They carried almost as much weight as the CAMS forecast itself and would have kept extrapolating that decline into November. Dropped.
  • obs_recent and obs_recent_log were the same signal twice, split across two coefficients that pulled against each other. One kept.
  • obs_age had been constant at 4.0 since the feed was repaired, so it contributed nothing but still cost a parameter. It is still published with each forecast. Since November it picks which model forecasts instead of being fitted on, as described above.
  • Thin days were being trained on. CPCB does not consider a 24-hour mean valid below 16 hourly readings, and neither should the model. Days under that line are recorded and displayed but are no longer used as labels, nor fed forward as a later day's persistence.

Two further changes did more than any of the above.

Fitting in log space. PM2.5 spans an order of magnitude between a clean day and a burning-season one. On the raw scale the squared error is decided by the worst few days, and the fit bends towards them at the expense of the ordinary ones. log1p makes the penalty proportional, which is also how the error is felt: ten out on a reading of twenty matters, ten out on two hundred does not.

Lagging the fire count. FIRMS records detections against the day they happened, so a target day's own count does not exist when its forecast goes out. It was a leak. Fixing it improved the model, because the physically correct signal was the lagged one all along — smoke lifted off a field upwind takes the better part of a day to arrive.

docs.title: A year and a half of history
docs.text:
Everything above was first fitted on about a hundred days, all of them summer and monsoon. The table began on 15 May 2026 because the bootstrap asked Open-Meteo for past_days=92, on the belief that this was as far back as the CAMS archive went. It was only the ceiling on that one parameter. The live sensor has reported since February 2025, so the 2025 burning season had been available from the start.

It mattered in October. On 3 and 5 October the live forecast was 22 µg/m³ against an observed 38: the model had never seen the season begin. scripts/extend_history.py pulled the table back to 19 February 2025, and every day of October and November 2025 came with it. Refitted on that history, the backtest gives 33 and 42 for the same two days. The data page has the details.

With a burning season in the table, four ways of letting the season change the model were tested against the current one by scripts/compare_models.py: interactions on fire count and eastward wind, on persistence and CAMS, all four, and a separate burning-season fit. The bar was fixed first: clearly better in burning season, no more than a point or two worse in calm. None cleared it, so the model is unchanged.

docs.title: The model lab
docs.text:
code/lab.py puts the shipped model next to every alternative worth trying, on the same days and with the same information.

  • Candidates. Three baselines (persistence, climatology, raw CAMS), then CAMS rescaled by its recent ratio to the station, the shipped ridge, ridge with the smoke terms from week 7, ridge corrected by half its mean error over the last seven published days, analog days (the average of the most similar past days), a random forest, gradient boosting, a small neural network, and an ensemble. The first eight need nothing outside the standard library and could ship. The scikit-learn models are benchmarks, installed for the lab alone (requirements-lab.txt).
  • Same rules for all. Every candidate is walked forward over the same days, from the same reading, and trains only on days whose readings had been published (evaluate.published). Anything that could ship is refitted daily, as the daily job would run it. The benchmarks are refitted weekly, because a daily refit of a forest takes minutes on its own.
  • Every reading age. The shipped model is also scored at ages two to seven days, which is how the cost of a slow feed is measured instead of guessed.
  • Shadow forecasts. Every morning each candidate issues its own forecast for tomorrow, frozen in data/shadow.json and scored when the observation lands. That builds a live record for each one, which no backtest can stand in for.

A challenger replaces the shipped model only if it passes all of the rule in lab.PROMOTION. It must be at least 3 points of skill better in burning season and no more than 2 points worse in calm season. Those two thresholds were written down in week 7. It must stay within 5% of the shipped model's error at every reading age from two to five days. And it must do no worse over 20 live days. Promotion is then a one-line change to config.SHIPPED_EXTRA in a pull request. Nothing in the lab changes what ships.

The age test was added for a reason. Ridge with the smoke terms clears the first two thresholds at two-day-old readings, but with three- and four-day-old readings it breaks down early in the 2025 season. With only a handful of burning days to learn from, the penalty chosen on a validation tail that contained none of them came out near zero, and one forecast for a day that measured 13 came out at 2684. A rule that only looked at one age would have shipped it.

docs.title: The likely range
docs.text:
Each forecast comes with a range meant to hold the measured value four days in five. It used to be built from the spread of the fit's own errors, which is narrower than the real spread by construction. It held 15 of the first 27 live days.

It is now the middle 80% of the backtest's out-of-sample errors, taken in log space and kept separate for each season (evaluate.calibrate). Under a log target the range comes out lopsided, wider above the forecast than below, which is the right shape for a quantity that spikes upward. Its honesty is checked the same way it is used (evaluate.coverage): each day's range is sized only from the days before it.

docs.title: The outlook
docs.text: Days two and three are forecast from the same station reading as tomorrow, so the reading is a day or two older for them, and each horizon gets a model fitted at that age. Their CAMS and weather come from the same morning's request and are kept in data/outlook.json rather than daily.csv, which only ever holds a day's day-ahead forecast. In the backtest the table has only day-ahead CAMS and weather for every horizon, which flatters days two and three a little; their live records are the check.

docs.title: Where it stands
docs.text:
Results is regenerated every morning and is the current evaluation, split by season, by reading age and by model, with a live-only line.

As of early November 2026, against persistence given the same two-day-old reading, the calm-season target is met and burning season is about a point short of its 20%. With readings four days old, the situation the proposal was written for, both are met comfortably. The shipped ridge and its smoke-term variant have the lowest errors of any single models on the leaderboard, ahead of the forest, boosting and the network. The model still does not see spikes coming. The analog list on the dashboard helps there: when tomorrow's inputs sit closest to past days that turned out Poor, a lower forecast deserves a second look.

There is no shuffled train/test split anywhere in this project; the rows are a time series and shuffling them would let the model read its own future.

The targets are set per season because the two are different problems. Calm-season air moves slowly and persistence is hard to beat; burning season is when a forecast is worth having.

docs.title: Skill
docs.text:
• Against operational persistence: 12.4% better on MAE.
  • Against textbook persistence: 12.5% worse on MAE.

The two baselines are both persistence, and the difference between them is the whole argument.

Operational persistence repeats the freshest reading the CPCB feed had published when the forecast went out, two days old at the reference age. That is the same information Pawan has, so it is a fair comparison, and it is what the forecast is worth to somebody deciding whether to run outside tomorrow.

Textbook persistence uses yesterday's reading. Nobody has yesterday's reading when the forecast goes out. It is reported because it is the figure quoted in the proposal, and because it marks the ceiling: the gap between the two baselines is the cost of the publication lag, and closing it needs a faster feed rather than a better model.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
What the figures above do not show.

  • Burning season is a small sample. 92 burning-season days are scored: 55 read back from archives and 37 recorded live. That is one or two seasons at most, and a dry year, a wet one or a shift in when the stubble is burnt would each move these numbers.
  • Band accuracy only means much in burning season. On calm days almost everything falls in Good, and a method that guessed Good every time would score nearly as well.
  • Archive rows are mildly optimistic. Rows read back from archives take CAMS and weather from series stitched out of the opening hours of successive model runs, which sit a little closer to what happened than a forecast issued a day ahead. The live-only figure, where there is one, is the check on how much that flatters the totals.
  • The feature set was chosen on calm-season data. Every change was made for a stated reason and not only because it scored better, but the reasons and the scores were looked at together. This year's burning season, scored live as it happens, is the test nothing here was tuned against.
  • The outlook's backtest is a little kind. The table keeps one CAMS and weather forecast per day, the day-ahead one, so days two and three are backtested with inputs better than they will have live. Their reading and fire count are moved back properly, which is the larger effect.

docs.title: Week 1 : Local Documentation Build Fails on a Fresh Clone
Hard-coded Toolchain Paths in the Template Makefile
docs.text: First week was introduction, so the only work was setting up. After forking the template and cloning it

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The template Makefile fixes its shell and Python environment at the top:

SHELL           := /usr/bin/zsh
ENV             := emacs
CONDA_ROOT      := ~/miniconda3

That assumes zsh at a specific path, Anaconda at ~/miniconda3, and a conda environment named emacs holding mkdocs. None of the three exists on a clean machine.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Two build configurations live in this repository and only one is a contract.

  • .github/workflows/mkdocs.yml installs its dependencies explicitly into a fresh runner, so it is reproducible by necessity.
  • The Makefile targets one developer's machine and is a convenience.

The real dependency list is therefore in the workflow file.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Reproduce the CI environment locally and skip the Makefile for this target:

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve

requirements-docs.txt is transcribed from the workflow and committed, so all three of us install the same set. .venv/ is gitignored. The Makefile is left untouched.

Because

Deriving the local environment from the CI specification keeps the two from drifting. If docs build locally but fail in CI, that difference is now a real signal rather than noise.

Leaving the Makefile alone matters separately: two report templates are still to be published upstream and will arrive by syncing the fork, so every file we edit unnecessarily is a file that can conflict later.

docs.title: A Promotion Rule That Only Looked At One Age
Error:
docs.text:
The first run of the model lab put ridge with the smoke terms at the top of the leaderboard. The smoke terms let the fire count and the westerly wind count for more in burning season. Against the rule written down in week 7, it passed: clearly better in burning season, no worse in calm.

                         MAE    calm     burning
shipped ridge            8.76   +13.2%   +18.9%
ridge + smoke terms      8.67   +13.4%   +22.1%

By that rule it should have shipped. The same model, scored with older station readings, said otherwise:

reading age   shipped ridge   ridge + smoke terms
2 days        8.76            8.67
3 days        9.13            10.65
4 days        9.43            15.50

The worst single day was 8 October 2025. The station measured 13.3 µg/m³. The smoke model forecast 2684.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
After the prototype review, the direction was more models with published comparisons. The week 7 script compared four variants of one ridge model at one reading age, and it trained each backtest step on days whose readings had not been published yet. Week 9 fixed that leak in the main backtest.

The feed's speed decides which reading age the forecast actually gets on a given morning (week 9). A model that only works at one age only works when the feed is on time.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
The blow-up came from the penalty search. Early in October 2025 the training set held only a few burning-season days, and the validation tail used to choose the penalty held none at all. On that tail the smoke terms were zero, so any penalty looked as good as any other, and the search picked almost none. The first real burning days then met weights that had never been held in check.

The lab's first version refitted every model weekly, to keep the tree models fast. That happened to skip those days. The daily job refits every morning, so a candidate that could ship has to be tested the way it would actually run.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
• code/candidates.py: eleven candidates behind one interface. Three baselines; CAMS rescaled; the shipped ridge; ridge with smoke terms; analog days, which average the most similar past days; a random forest, gradient boosting and a small neural network from scikit-learn; and an ensemble. The standard-library ones could ship. The scikit-learn ones are benchmarks, imported only inside their fits.
  • code/lab.py walks every candidate forward over the same days, with training cut at the last published reading. Anything that could ship is refitted daily and the benchmarks weekly. The shipped model is also scored at every reading age from two to seven days.
  • The promotion rule is written in code (lab.PROMOTION) and printed on the results page. The week 7 thresholds come first. Then the challenger must stay within 5% of the shipped model's error at every age from two to five days, and do no worse over 20 days of live forecasts. Promotion itself is a one-line change to config.SHIPPED_EXTRA, made in a pull request.
  • Every model now issues a shadow forecast each morning, frozen in data/shadow.json, so each one builds a live record alongside the real forecast.
  • The likely range is now the middle 80% of the backtest's own out-of-sample errors, per season, instead of the fit's in-sample spread. Sized only from earlier days, it held 355 of 440 backtest days (81%), and 54 of 76 in burning season (71%), where a new season starts with the fewest errors to size from.
  • A three-day outlook: days two and three from the same reading, each with a model fitted at that reading's age, frozen like tomorrow's forecast.
  • The dashboard gained the outlook, a "days like tomorrow" list, the leaderboard with what every model says about tomorrow, a chart of error against reading age, and the range's hit rate.

The leaderboard now reads:
